Understanding the automatic quality checks

Source: vignettes/Curation-Flags.Rmd
Curation-Flags.Rmd

After it annotates a sample, RiboPilot runs a set of automatic quality checks and raises a flag for anything that looks unusual. Flags are there to guide your attention: they point out samples worth a closer look in the app’s Annotate tab. They do not change your data, and a flag does not always mean something is wrong. It just means “please check this”.

You will see flags in two places in the app: a small count next to each sample in the table, and a detailed Curation flags panel when you open a sample. Each flag links to the exact feature it concerns, so you can jump straight to it.

What the flags mean

Flag Applies to What it means
missing_18S, missing_5.8S, missing_28S sample One of the three ribosomal genes was not found.
missing_ITS1, missing_ITS2 sample A spacer was not recovered between its neighboring genes.
out_of_order sample The five features are not in the expected order (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S).
overlap feature Two features overlap when they should sit side by side.
wrong_strand feature A feature was found on the opposite strand from what is expected.
length feature A feature is shorter or longer than typical for your group.
low_identity feature A conserved gene is less similar to reference sequences than expected (could signal an assembly problem or a genuinely unusual sample).
contaminant sample The closest published match belongs to an unrelated group, which can indicate contamination.

The last two checks (low_identity and contaminant) rely on looking up a reference match on NCBI during assembly. If that lookup was unavailable at the time, those two checks are simply skipped and the others still apply.

How the checks are tuned per group

Some checks, especially the expected lengths, depend on the group of organisms. RiboPilot ships two settings:

  • Generic animal (the default): deliberately wide length ranges that suit a broad range of animals.
  • Fish: tighter, fish-specific ranges for the ribosomal genes, with the spacers kept wide because they vary even between close relatives.

For reference, the generic animal length ranges are:

Feature Typical length (bases)
18S 1600 - 2100
5.8S 140 - 180
28S 2000 - 6000 (the recovered portion varies with sequencing depth)
ITS1 120 - 1600
ITS2 120 - 1600

A length flag simply means a feature fell outside these ranges. That is common and often fine, especially for the fast-evolving spacers; it is a prompt to look, not a verdict.

Adding tuning for a new group

If you work on a group that would benefit from its own length ranges, that can be added. This is a small change to RiboPilot’s settings rather than new analysis code. If you are comfortable with R you can add it yourself (see rrna_params() in the source), but you are also very welcome to open an issue describing your group, and we can help set it up. In the meantime, the generic animal setting works for any group; it is just more lenient.
